latin.354: PLAC. Scriptura nunquam corruptionem, aut corruptionis propagationem judicio Dei ascribit. itaque non agitur de locutione Scripturae, sed Theologorum, accipienda, pro eo ac pati potest analogia fidei & rei natura, in meliorem potius quam in detriorem partem. Quod si justi judicii nomine nihil aliud intellexerunt, quam opus illud Dei, quo poenam aliquam ex ratione justitiae vindicatricis irrogat, revera intellexerunt judicium Dei contra homines. Sed omne Dei judicium contra homines quia sunt peccatores, supponit eos esse peccatores, non facit. Hic autem agitur de judicio Dei, quod antecedit peccatum hominum, qui absque eo forent, peccatores non essent.
latin.355: Non sunt igitur ad propositum quae afferuntur exempla. In illis enim agitur de judicio sequente eorum, quibus poena irrogatur, peccatum. Hic vero quaestio est de judicio, antecedente eorum qui puniuntur, peccatum. Deinde censuitne vir doctus, hanc esse judicii Dei perpetuam in Scriptura significationem, necne? Si censuit, erravit: non raro enim aliter accipitur, ut patet ex Ps. 119. 7. 12. 19. 29. &c. Si non censuit, quorsum eiusmodi loca laudavit? & quam vim habere possunt ad me refellendum?
latin.356: GAR. Quid quod nihil est omnino in totius mundi gubernatione, quod inscio, vel invito Deo fiat, quod sine permissione Dei eveniat, ubi non Dei sapientia eluceat, quod non juste, id est, ex immota & indeflexa Dei rectitudine administretur? Neque tamen propterea dicet aliquis haec fieri ex occulto, justo, admirabili, inscrutabili, Dei consilio, etiam cum arbores crescunt, & prata variegantur floribus, & animalia propagant speciem, & vermes ex terra formantur. Sunt enim certe illa omnia ex sapientia & providentia, eaque rectissima & consultissima. Sed justum, occultum, mirabile Dei consilium, non ad communem eiusmodi rerum creatarum administrationem Scriptura referre solet, sed ad singularem in certis operibus dispensationem & oeconomiam: ut cum dicit Paulus Roman. XI. 33. judicia Dei esse inscrutabilia, & vias eius impervestigabiles.
latin.357: PLAC. Primum non quaeritur hoc loco quid soleat Scriptura ad Dei judicium referre. Non enim, ut iam observavi, ullo loco propagationem originalis peccati ad Dei judicium retulit. Quaeritur tantum quo sensu non repugnante Scriptura, & rationi possit referri. Alium certe sensum, qui cum Scriptura & recta ratione conciliari possit, non video, praeter eum, quem hoc loco & in fine cap. 12. & paulo ante medium cap. 13. huius ipsius Manuscripti exposui.
latin.358: Caeterum contra se vir doctus laudasse videtur verba illa Apostoli, judicia Dei sunt inscrutabilia, & viae eius impervestigabiles. Constat enim eo loco per judicia Dei non intelligi opera Dei, quibus poenam ex ratione justitiae vindicatricis irrogat, ut vult vir doctus: nam neque de eiusmodi operibus agebatur eo loco, neque eiusmodi judicia solent esse impervestigabilia: quippe quorum ratio in Dei justitia, & peccatis hominum est aperta.
latin.359: GAR. Tertio cum in hac causa Calvinus & Theologi haec duo opponunt, fieri ex vi naturae, & fieri ex ratione judicii divini; quomodo vir doctus illud fieri dicit justo Dei judicio, quod fit ita naturaliter, ut impediri non possit, nisi contra naturae ordinem, & nisi evertantur leges naturalis propagationis, & nisi sistatur, & sufflaminetur peccati actualis sequela & efficacia naturalis?

pass_a.354: Placeus: Scripture never ascribes corruption or its propagation to God's judgment—so the fight is over theologians' locution, to be taken by analogy of faith toward the better sense. If 'just judgment' means only the vindicative work that inflicts punishment, that is judgment against men as sinners—which presupposes sinners, it does not make them. Here the judgment in question antecedes the sin of men who without it would not be sinners.
pass_a.355: The cited examples are therefore off purpose: they treat judgment following the sin of those punished. Here the question is judgment anteeding the punished's sin. If GAR thought 'judgment of God' always means that in Scripture, he erred—Ps. 119:7, 12, 19, 29 take it otherwise. If he did not think so, why praise those places, and what force have they against Placeus?
pass_a.356: GAR presses that nothing at all in the government of the whole world happens with God unknowing or unwilling, without his permission, without his wisdom shining, or without just administration from unmoved rectitude—yet no one therefore says tree-growth, flowered meadows, animal propagation, or worms formed from earth come from occult, admirable, inscrutable counsel; those are ordinary most-right providence. Scripture reserves just, occult, marvelous counsel for singular dispensation and economy in certain works, as when Paul at Rom. 11:33 calls God's judgments inscrutable and his ways past finding out.
pass_a.357: Placeus answers that the question here is not what Scripture is accustomed to refer to God's judgment; as he already observed, it never in any place refers the propagation of original sin to God's judgment. Ask only in what sense—Scripture not resisting and reason allowing—it can be referred. He sees no other sense reconcilable with Scripture and right reason besides the one he set out in this place and in this same Manuscript at the end of cap. 12 and a little before the middle of cap. 13.
pass_a.358: For the rest, Placeus says GAR seems to have praised against himself the Apostle's words that God's judgments are inscrutable and his ways past finding out. In that Romans place, 'judgments of God' are not the works by which God inflicts punishment from vindicative justice as GAR wills—for neither was such work the subject there, nor are such punishing judgments usually past finding out, since their reason in God's justice and in men's sins stands open. Tip before GAR's Tertio on Calvin.
pass_a.359: GAR opens Tertio: Calvin and the school set nature's force against divine judgment's reason as opposed explanations. He asks how Placeus can still call the corruption-spread God's just judgment when it runs so naturally that blocking it would mean fighting nature's order, overturning propagation laws, and choking off actual sin's natural follow-through. Tip into Placeus's Calvin reading.

354: PLAC. Scripture never ascribes corruption, or the propagation of corruption, to God's judgment. And so it is not a matter of Scripture's locution, but of the Theologians', to be taken insofar as the analogy of faith and the nature of the thing can bear, toward the better rather than the worse part. But if by the name of just judgment they understood nothing other than that work of God by which he inflicts some punishment from the reason of vindicative justice, they truly understood the judgment of God against men. But every judgment of God against men because they are sinners presupposes that they are sinners; it does not make them so. Here, however, the question is of a judgment of God that antecedes the sin of men who, without it, would not be sinners.
355: Therefore the examples brought forward are not to the purpose. For in those it is a matter of judgment following the sin of those on whom punishment is inflicted. Here the question is of a judgment anteeding the sin of those who are punished. Next, did the learned man think this is the perpetual signification of God's judgment in Scripture, or not? If he thought so, he erred: for not rarely it is taken otherwise, as is plain from Ps. 119:7, 12, 19, 29, &c. If he did not think so, to what end did he praise such places? and what force can they have to refute me?
356: GAR. What of this—that there is nothing at all in the government of the whole world that is done with God unknowing or unwilling, that happens without God's permission, where God's wisdom does not shine, that is not administered justly, that is, from God's unmoved and undeflected rectitude? Yet no one will therefore say these things are done from God's occult, just, admirable, inscrutable counsel even when trees grow, and meadows are varied with flowers, and animals propagate their species, and worms are formed from the earth. For those things certainly are all from wisdom and providence, and that most right and most consulted. But Scripture is accustomed to refer God's just, occult, marvelous counsel not to the common administration of such created things, but to a singular dispensation and economy in certain works: as when Paul says, Rom. 11:33, that God's judgments are inscrutable and his ways past finding out.
357: PLAC. First, it is not asked in this place what Scripture is accustomed to refer to God's judgment. For, as I have already observed, it has in no place referred the propagation of original sin to God's judgment. It is asked only in what sense, Scripture not resisting, and reason allowing, it can be referred. Certainly I see no other sense that can be reconciled with Scripture and right reason besides that which I have set out in this place and at the end of cap. 12 and a little before the middle of cap. 13 of this same Manuscript.
358: For the rest, the learned man seems to have praised against himself those words of the Apostle, the judgments of God are inscrutable, and his ways past finding out. For it is clear that in that place by God's judgments are not understood God's works by which he inflicts punishment from the reason of vindicative justice, as the learned man wills: for neither was it a matter of such works in that place, nor are such judgments accustomed to be past finding out—seeing that their reason in God's justice and in men's sins is open.
359: GAR. Third, since in this cause Calvin and the Theologians oppose these two—to be done by the force of nature, and to be done from the reason of divine judgment—how does the learned man say that is done by God's just judgment which is done so naturally that it cannot be hindered except against the order of nature, and unless the laws of natural propagation are overturned, and unless the sequel and natural efficacy of actual sin is stopped and checked?
